title: The resurrection and the life
hook: Jesus tells Martha: I am the resurrection and the life (John 11:25)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a time to be born and a time to die. Your line was a time for everything. What season did you name? Today closes the week, with Christian voices, and a sister standing on a road. Day seven hundred seventy-seven.

A house in Bethany, near Jerusalem. A man named Lazarus has died. His sisters, Martha and Mary, had sent word to their friend Jesus while Lazarus was still sick. He came late. When he arrives, John's Gospel says, Lazarus has already lain in the grave four days. Martha hears that Jesus is on the road and goes out to meet him. Mary stays in the house. Martha's first words are the ones a grieving person says at a hospital door: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died."
screen: `LAZARUS HAS DIED.` → `JESUS COMES LATE.` → `MARTHA GOES OUT TO MEET HIM.`

segments.voice: First, Martha already hopes. When Jesus tells her that her brother will rise again, she answers with what she knows: "I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day." Her hope is real, but it's far away, at the end of everything. It doesn't help much on day fifteen. Second, I am. Jesus answers: "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live." In John's telling, the hope Martha placed at the end of time is suddenly standing in front of her on a dusty road, with a name and a face. Third, a question, and tears. Jesus asks her plainly: "Believest thou this?" Martha says yes, and names him the Christ. Then, on the way to the tomb, before anything is mended, two words: "Jesus wept." Only after the weeping does he call, "Lazarus, come forth," and the dead man walks out still wrapped in grave clothes. Christians read this as a sign, a return to this life. The hope they hold is larger: that because Jesus himself rose from the dead, the dead will be raised. Churches describe the details in their own ways, and in some churches this line is read at funerals and spoken at gravesides. Fourth, the week. Nachiketa's question at Death's door. The fires on the ghats. A mourner's prayer of praise. Neighbors who come to the house. Numbered days. A time for everything. And today, one tradition's hope said out loud. Whether or not it's your hope, it can be heard as Christians say it: christians hope this.
screen: `MARTHA HOPES FOR THE LAST DAY.` · `"I AM THE RESURRECTION."` · `A QUESTION, THEN TEARS.` · `A WEEK OF ANSWERS TO DEATH.` · then, large: `CHRISTIANS HOPE THIS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Hear Martha's first line again: if you had been here. Notice how ordinary it is, the sentence of anyone who arrived too late or watched someone else arrive too late. Then hear the answer Jesus gives in John's Gospel: I am the resurrection, and the life. You don't have to do anything with it. Just let it sit beside Martha's grief for a while, the hope and the tears in the same scene. If you pray, you can carry Martha's words into the quiet. The bell holds the time.
The resurrection and the life: what Jesus calls himself to Martha in John's Gospel, the center of the Christian hope that the dead will be raised. Today's word.
screen: `THE RESURRECTION AND THE LIFE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: christians hope this. Today, if you pass a church or hear a hymn, remember Martha on the road, hoping and grieving at once. Day seven hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Some churches read John 11 at funerals, and in some burial services the words "I am the resurrection, and the life" are spoken at the graveside.

fork.setup: you're Martha. your brother is four days in the grave and the friend you sent for has finally come. what do you do?
options: stay in the house and refuse to see him.
go out to meet him and say, if you had been here.
send a message telling him not to bother.
fork.reveal: Martha goes out on the road, says it plainly, and hears: I am the resurrection, and the life.

trapdoor: what you thought: the resurrection is the story of Lazarus walking out of his tomb.
what it means: Jesus names himself the resurrection and the life; Christians hope the dead will be raised.
what a scholar hears: John moves Martha's hope from "the last day" to a person in front of her: "I am."

notes: No superlative used for John 11:35 (claims rule).
'This line is read at Christian funerals and spoken at gravesides' (and howItsDone 'in many churches'): confirm wording, e.g. BCP 1662 burial service opens with John 11:25–26.
'Churches describe the details in their own ways' is deliberately general (intermediate state, nature of the resurrection body).
Original left null: Greek anastasis was considered but no etymology is taught under the claims rule.

Audit: 'Jesus wept' moved from 'at the tomb' to 'on the way to the tomb' (John 11:34–38: he weeps, then comes to the grave) in the teach, match and myth; garbled practice line 'the answer John gives Jesus' fixed.
Editor: softened 'often read at Christian funerals' and howItsDone 'in many churches' to 'some churches' (claims rule); quotations checked against KJV John 11.
